newsitem.title: CHINA: China price index marks step towards transparency.
newsitem.headline: China price index marks step towards transparency.

text.p: The unveiling of a new price index by the central People's Bank of China shows the bank's confidence in checking inflation and marks a step toward greater transparency, officials and analysts said on Thursday.
The newly announced index, which the central bank has used internally since 1987, gauges the purchase prices of materials used for production, including raw materials and fuel.
"We announced the index to let everyone in society know," said a People's Bank official, who declined to be identified. "The index is very useful."
China's State Statistical Bureau already releases a monthly retail price index and a consumer price index, which is a broader measure of inflation than the retail index since it includes services.

The publicising of the production material price index after 10 years of internal dissemination also shows the central bank feels secure in making such figures known after bringing down roaring inflation in the last year, analysts said.

Chinese authorities have been battling to control inflation since it soared to a communist-era high of 21.7 percent for benchmark retail price inflation in 1994, fearing public discontent could trigger social unrest.
"One of the reasons that they're releasing it now is that inflation has come down," one Western analyst said.
China's retail prices rose 0.8 percent in May compared with the same month in 1996, while consumer prices rose 2.8 percent, the State Statistical Bureau has said.

"Any time China releases a new data series it's a step towards becoming more transparent," said John Seel, sovereign analyst for Bear Stearns Asia Ltd in Hong Kong. "But they have a lot more steps to go."

Analysts said they question the accuracy of China's price measures because the government does not specify what is included in the basket of items that make up the indices, their specific weightings and the methods of calculation.
The inclusion of items with fixed prices, which still exist under China's partly planned economy, would distort the accuracy of the indices, they said.

"It (the newly announced index) won't be highly indicative unless we know what the components are and what the weighting of each is," said Alex Conroy, a senior investment analyst for ING Barings in Shanghai.
"But another statistic is one small step forward," she said.
The central bank will use the production price index as a tool to gauge inflation and set monetary policy, one official said. The index level will be announced monthly, he said.
The index stood at 99.53 points in May, based on 100 for the same month last year, indicating production material prices were down 0.47 percent last month, the official said.
The raw material component of the index fell 2.45 percent in May compared with the same month in 1996, while the fuel portion rose 7.84 percent, according to central bank statistics.
